query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting Ta with Nb in the alloy—thus converting as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr into HfMoNbTiZr—will reduce the overall density without sacrificing the high strength and ductility at room temperature and around 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast, near‐equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy with a density of about 10.21 g/cm³ exhibiting high strength at both room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by replacing Ta with Nb (i.e. use Hf, Mo, Nb, Ti, and Zr in near-equiatomic ratios) while keeping processing conditions similar to the original as-cast preparation.
generation.conditions: Mechanical property evaluations (e.g., tensile and/or compressive tests) conducted at room temperature and at elevated temperatures near 1000 °C under standard loading rates in inert or controlled atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of a single-phase, solid-solution (likely BCC) structure where atomic interactions and lattice distortion are maintained; the chemical substitution reduces the mean density due to the lower density of Nb compared to Ta.
generation.mechanism: By replacing the heavy Ta (density ~16.7 g/cm³) with significantly lighter Nb (density ~8.6 g/cm³) while preserving similar high-melting and strengthening characteristics, the overall density of the alloy is reduced. The substitution is expected to maintain solid solution strengthening and phase stability, thus preserving the excellent mechanical properties at both room and elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified HfMoNbTiZr alloy should have a lower density (well below 10.21 g/cm³) while exhibiting yield strengths, ultimate strengths, and ductility at both room temperature and around 1000 °C comparable to those of the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
generation.baseline: The as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy, known for its high strength at room temperature and elevated temperatures (~1000 °C) but having a high density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to as-cast, near-equiatomic refractory high-entropy alloys prepared via conventional casting routes and tested under typical laboratory mechanical testing conditions (room temperature and ~1000 °C) with standard strain rates; it assumes maintenance of a stable single-phase BCC (or similar) microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: While literature suggests that Nb can supplement high-temperature strength and ductility similar to Ta, the exact quantitative retention of mechanical properties (strength and ductility) and potential subtle microstructural changes during solidification remain uncertain until experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a near-equiatomic HfMoNbTiZr alloy via the same casting process as the original HfMoTaTiZr. Employ X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to confirm that the alloy retains a single-phase solid-solution structure. Perform density measurements (using the Archimedes method) and mechanical tests (tensile and/or compression tests) at room temperature and at approximately 1000 °C in an inert or controlled atmosphere.
measurements: Phase identification and microstructural characterization (XRD, SEM)
Room-temperature yield strength, ultimate tensile/compressive strength, and ductility
Elevated-temperature (≈1000 °C) mechanical properties (yield strength and ductility)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HfMoNbTiZr alloy shows a significant reduction (e.g., >10–15% drop) in yield strength or ductility at either room temperature or at 1000 °C relative to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr baseline, or if unwanted phase formation/segregation is detected, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo.
